newsitem.title: GERMANY: BUNDS TO FIND SHORT-TERM RELIEF IN FIXED REPO.
newsitem.headline: BUNDS TO FIND SHORT-TERM RELIEF IN FIXED REPO.

text.p: German Bund futures bounced back from a period of weakness on Tuesday as the Bundesbank calmed nerves by leaving its main money market rate, the repo, fixed at 3.00 percent.
The move, which quietened widespread speculation about an imminent credit tightening in Germany, allowed the DTB September future to reach levels not seen for a week.
But analysts said that although rates were on hold for now, the speculation had not been quashed altogether and was likely to resume ahead of the central bank's next repo announcement next Tuesday.
"The speculation isn't going away," said Charles Diebel, senior fixed income analyst at Technical Data in London. "The Bundesbank loves to keep people guessing after all."
"But the economic fundamentals don't argue for higher rates, so it depends really on how desperate the Bundesbank gets about dollar/mark," he added.
The dollar, which has stabilised against the mark in recent session, was trading at 1.8645/40 marks by 1408 GMT.
For the moment, however, the long end of the Bund market would be led into firmer ground by futures, with the mood improved by Tuesday's Bundesbank decision, analysts said.
The September DTB future was trading at 102.20 by 1410 GMT, up 27 basis points on the day but down from its earlier peak of 102.33.
Technical analysts said the key level for the Bund future was 102.17. A close above there this session would allow scope for further gains in the coming days.
"Dips are buys from here, and as long as 102.17 holds, pressure to go higher should keep up towards the 102.51 area," said one. The future plotted a day's high at 102.51 on July 15.
On the fundamental side, analysts said the U.S. would become the main focus in coming sessions.

U.S. retail sales and producer price data for July are due on Wednesday, while consumer prices, business inventories, weekly jobless claims, real earnings and a clutch of other data are due on Thursday.
"Retail sales could be a bit ugly tomorrow, which opens up the possibility of a dip in Bunds," said Diebel.
Economists polled by Reuters are forecasting a 0.7 percent month-on-month rise in U.S. retail sales in July, up from 0.5 percent in June.
